title: Cool-Season Grasses: Lawn Maintenance Calendar (G6705)
authors: Peng Tian (rev. April 2025); orig. D.D. Miner & J.H. Dunn
takeaway: September is "the most important time to fertilize" (1–1.5 lb N/1,000 sq ft), with a second feeding in mid-October; fall feedings can replace spring. "Do not apply nitrogen fertilizer… past May 1." Tall fescue mowing: 2–3.5 in spring, 3–4 in summer, 2.5–3.5 in fall. Crabgrass preventer by April 15. Lime only at pH 5.8 or lower, up to 50 lb/1,000 per application. Treat grubs at 5–10 per sq ft.

title: Cool-Season Grasses: Lawn Establishment and Renovation (G6700)
authors: Peng Tian, Manoj Chhetri & Brad Fresenburg (reviewed Oct 2022)
takeaway: Best seeding window is Aug 25–Oct 10; lawns seeded within a week of Labor Day fill in best. Tall fescue: 7 lb/1,000 in fall (10 in spring). Spring seeding "can be extremely difficult." Wait one month after 2,4-D/dicamba/mecoprop before seeding; 7 days after glyphosate.

title: Managing Lawns and Turfgrass (MG10, Missouri Master Gardener Core Manual)
authors: Brad Fresenburg & Lee Miller (reviewed May 2016)
takeaway: Turf-type tall fescue: 7–9 lb seed/1,000 sq ft; time seeding for Labor Day weekend (possible until Oct 15). Forage-type fescue belongs on roadsides (10 lb if used). Tall fescue needs ~0.8 in/week to stay green, ~0.5 in/week to survive dormant; "dormant lawns should receive at least 1 inch of water every two to three weeks during summer to prevent complete turf loss."

title: Vegetable Planting Calendar (G6201)
authors: David H. Trinklein (rev.)
takeaway: Spring and fall planting windows for ~50 vegetables in North, Central and South Missouri. The Kansas City metro falls in the Central region (Figure 1).

title: Growing Home Garden Tomatoes (G6461)
authors: David Trinklein (rev. May 2022)
takeaway: Central Missouri: set tomatoes out about May 5–20, once soil is above 60°F. "Plants may be set out several days to a week earlier if gardeners are willing to protect them from a possible frost."

title: Squash: Recognition at Last (squash vine borer control)
org: MU Integrated Pest Management — Missouri Environment & Garden
authors: David Trinklein
takeaway: "To prevent borer damage, insecticides must be applied at the base of the plant before the larva enter the stem. Once inside, insecticides are of little control value."

title: Trap cropping: a simple, effective and affordable IPM strategy
org: MU IPM — Missouri Environment & Garden (Lincoln University)
authors: Jaime Piñero
takeaway: Squash vine borers emerge and lay eggs at the base of plants around June in mid-Missouri. "Blue Hubbard squash is very attractive to squash bugs and to squash vine borer, and therefore it is an excellent trap crop plant."

title: Trap Cropping to Control Cucumber Beetles and Squash Bugs in Cucurbit Crops (GS#18-G-2017)
authors: Jaime C. Piñero
takeaway: A border of Blue Hubbard squash draws cucumber beetles and squash bugs away from the main crop, so you treat only the border.

title: Garlic: A Brief History
org: MU Integrated Pest Management — Missouri Environment & Garden
authors: David Trinklein
takeaway: "October is an ideal month to plant garlic in Missouri." (A 2022 MU IPM article says late September into October is the popular window.) Buy seed garlic, not supermarket bulbs.

title: Prune oak trees this winter to avoid oak wilt
authors: quoting Hank Stelzer, MU state forestry specialist
takeaway: Oaks can be infected by the oak wilt fungus if pruned during the high-risk period, mid-March through mid-July. Winter is safe: beetles that spread it aren't active.

title: Oak Wilt
takeaway: "Avoid pruning or damaging oaks from mid-March through June."

title: Battling Japanese beetles in your garden and flowers
takeaway: MU does not recommend traps, "which will actually attract more beetles to your yard." Hand-pick into soapy water in the morning.

title: Japanese Beetles in the Urban Landscape (ENTFACT-451)
authors: D.A. Potter, M.F. Potter & L.H. Townsend
takeaway: Research showed "the traps attract many more beetles than are actually caught"; in most landscapes they "probably will do more harm than good."

title: MU Soil and Plant Testing Laboratory
takeaway: Regular fertility test with lawn- or garden-specific recommendations (lb of nutrient and lime per 1,000 sq ft). Submit through your county Extension office or by mail.

title: MU Extension county offices
takeaway: Your county Extension office: soil test drop-off, horticulture questions and classes.

title: Lawn calendar for cool-season grasses
authors: Matt McKernan
takeaway: Avoid early spring fertilizer. Crabgrass preventer when redbuds are in full bloom, watered in. Fertilize in May only if you water or rainfall keeps the lawn from going dormant. Grub prevention: chlorantraniliprole in May or imidacloprid May–June; Dylox for active damage. Fertilize and core aerate around Labor Day; seed late August–mid-October. November: high-nitrogen feeding and broadleaf spraying "even if they are small."

title: Tall Fescue Lawns (MF736)
authors: Jared Hoyle et al.
takeaway: "Siduron (Tupersan) and mesotrione (Tenacity) are the only two preemergence crabgrass preventers that can be safely applied at seeding time." Avoid broadleaf killers until new grass has been mowed three times. Best planting: mid-September; 6–8 lb/1,000 sq ft (3–5 to overseed).

title: Brown Patch in Tall Fescue Lawns: Information for Homeowners
authors: Megan Kennelly
takeaway: The fungus takes off when nights stay above 65°F with dew and humidity, often in July–August. Put most fertilizer in fall (Sep–Nov), use slow-release in spring, mow at 3–3.5 in, and don't overseed at excessive rates.

title: Nitrogen rate and fungicide had big impact on brown patch in tall fescue this summer
short: K-State Turf blog: N & brown patch
authors: Jack Fry
takeaway: Tall fescue fed 4.5 lb N/yr (1 lb April, 1 lb May, 1.5 lb Sept, 1 lb Nov) declined quickly in July without fungicide; a single 1.5-lb September feeding "had little brown patch even when fungicides were not applied."

title: Methods of predicting crabgrass emergence
authors: Jared Hoyle
takeaway: Apply pre-emergent around when soil at 1 in has held ~55°F for about 5 days (~200 growing degree days, base 50°F); plant cues like redbud bloom track this.

title: Recommended Vegetable Varieties (L41)
authors: Ward Upham
takeaway: Kansas-tested varieties for every major crop, e.g. El Jefe and TAM jalapeños; Celebrity, Big Beef and Jet Star tomatoes; Crimson Sweet and Sugar Baby watermelons; Music, Chesnok Red and Purple Glazer garlic.

title: Pine Diseases in Kansas: Tip Blight, Dothistroma Needle Blight, and Pine Wilt (L722)
authors: Megan Kennelly
takeaway: Cut a pine-wilt tree "by May 1 at the latest, before the beetles emerge. April 1 is a better deadline." Cut to the ground and chip or burn it immediately; don't keep it for firewood. Scots pine is especially susceptible.

title: Problem: Blossom-end Rot
takeaway: Low soil calcium is "rare in Kansas"; blossom-end rot usually follows moisture swings, sudden heat, drought stress or root damage that limit calcium uptake. "Do not assume that blossom-end rot is sure evidence that the soil lacks calcium."

title: For Professionals: Herbicide Delays after Seeding
authors: Zac Reicher
takeaway: Tenacity: "Prior to seeding, or four weeks or two mowings after emergence whichever is longer." Most broadleaf products: new turf "should be mowed 2-4 times prior to treatment." Purdue's AY-10 adds: "Do not use preemergence herbicides on new seedlings or before seeding an area."

title: Water Wise: Drought Effects on Turf in the Landscape (G2191)
authors: Jim A. Schild & Scott Dworak
takeaway: "Turfgrasses can typically survive dormancy periods of four to five weeks; however, if temperatures are continually greater than 80°F, survival is greatly reduced after three to four weeks. Applying ¼ to ½ inch of water every two to three weeks will help ensure hydration of the crowns while not greening up the dormant turf."

title: Native Landscape Care Calendar
takeaway: Leave stems and seed heads over winter; in spring cut stems to 8–24 in of stubble so stem-nesting native bees have places to lay eggs. Give asters and goldenrods a 25–75% "spring haircut" in late April–early May for compact plants.

title: Ornamental Grasses (factsheet)
takeaway: Cut ornamental grasses back to a few inches in late winter or early spring, "just before new spring growth has begun." Divide in spring before growth begins, or in late summer/fall.

title: Emerald Ash Borer Management Guide for Missouri Homeowners
org: Missouri Department of Conservation / Missouri Dept. of Agriculture
takeaway: Consider treating when EAB is within 15 miles or in your county (it is in the Kansas City area). Trees under 20 in diameter: DIY imidacloprid soil drench in early spring (about late March–mid April), most effective under 15 in. Larger trees need a professional trunk injection.

title: Japanese Beetles
takeaway: Traps don't catch all the beetles they attract; if you use one, place it at least 100 feet from plants you want to protect.

title: Physiological indicators associated with drought tolerance and post-drought recovery in tall fescue
short: Abtahi 2026: tall fescue drought recovery traits
authors: Abtahi M., Majidi M.M., Taleb H. & Behrooz A.R.
takeaway: In a field trial in arid Isfahan, Iran, cutting water reduced tall fescue yield 18–34% and leaf pigments 5–28%. Plants that recovered best after a two-month drought had more stored carbohydrate and stronger antioxidant defenses, and those traits are heritable, so breeders can select for them.
caveat: Forage-type breeding lines measured for yield, not lawn quality, and they aren't sold as seed. Read it as a sign of where drought breeding is heading.

title: Adaptability and character traits of turf-type tall fescue cultivars grown under limited irrigation in northern Italy
short: Novello 2025: tall fescue cultivars on limited irrigation
authors: Novello A., Pornaro C., Fidanza M. & Macolino S.
takeaway: Twenty turf-type tall fescues got no irrigation for two years after establishment, apart from one emergency watering. All held up, with only a slight drop in quality in the drier second summer. PPG-TF336 (sold as Raptor LS), Triad and ZRC-1 (Spyder 2LS) led on quality and green cover. The darkest-green cultivars did worst in summer and winter.
caveat: Po Valley climate with milder winters than KC; mowed at 2 in. The retail names are matched to NTEP breeder codes.

title: Minimum water requirements of cool-season turfgrasses for survival and recovery after prolonged drought
short: Hong 2021 (K-State): minimum water to survive drought
authors: Hong M., Bremer D.J. & Keeley S.
takeaway: Under rain-out shelters in Manhattan, KS, tall fescue fully recovered from 60–83-day droughts even with zero water, while Kentucky bluegrass sod did not recover. Watering at 50% of ET kept tall fescue acceptable 15–43 days longer and sped recovery.
caveat: The shelters excluded all rain, which is harsher than a real KC summer, and the sod was in its first summer.

title: Response of drought susceptible and resistant Kentucky bluegrass and tall fescue cultivars and mixtures to limited irrigation
short: Powlen 2022 (Purdue): fescue & bluegrass on limited irrigation
authors: Powlen J.S., Patton A.J., Jiang Y., Fraser M.L. & Bigelow C.A.
takeaway: Tall fescue and 90:10 tall fescue:bluegrass mixtures stayed green longest when water was limited, and drought-resistant tall fescue cultivars needed the least water. Mowing at 2 vs 3.5 in generally made no difference.
caveat: Indiana (Purdue). Tested limited irrigation, not recovery from full dormancy.

title: Response of tall fescue and Kentucky bluegrass mixtures to wear
authors: Park B.S., Samaranayake H. & Murphy J.A.
takeaway: Lawns seeded 90:10 tall fescue:bluegrass by weight ended up 37–79% tall fescue, depending on the bluegrass cultivar. The mixtures had less brown patch than tall fescue alone.
caveat: New Jersey (Rutgers).

title: Turf performance of mixtures and blends of tall fescue, Kentucky bluegrass, and perennial ryegrass
authors: Dunn J.H., Ervin E.H. & Fresenburg B.S.
takeaway: After 5 years in Columbia, MO, tall fescue made up 62% of tall fescue + bluegrass mixtures. Bluegrass competed better where irrigated than where rain-fed, and mixing sometimes reduced disease.
caveat: Older cultivars and low mowing heights (0.75 and 2 in).

title: Sod strength and rhizome characteristics of rhizomatous tall fescue
authors: Nwachukwu E.U., Fry J.D., Domenghini J.C. & Braun R.C.
takeaway: After 4.3 months, "rhizomatous" tall fescue rhizomes averaged 3.1 mm or less, versus more than 80 mm for Kentucky bluegrass. Don't pay extra expecting RTF to fill in bare spots.
caveat: Rhizomes were measured in a controlled environment; sod strength in the field.

title: Establishment rate and lateral spread of Festuca arundinacea cultivars
short: St. John 2009 (K-State): tall fescue lateral spread
authors: St. John R., Fry J., Bremer D. & Keeley S.
takeaway: Kentucky bluegrass nearly closed 12-in bare spots in 21 months. Every tall fescue, including a rhizomatous blend, still had gaps of more than 7 in, so reseed bare spots in a fescue lawn instead of waiting for them to fill.
caveat: 2009-era cultivars.

title: Species succession and turf quality of tall fescue and Kentucky bluegrass mixtures as affected by mowing height
authors: Macolino S., Pignata G., Giolo M. & Richardson M.D.
takeaway: In Italy, tall fescue + bluegrass mixtures containing rhizomatous tall fescue had higher quality and density than those with standard tall fescue. That's the most favorable RTF result, and it conflicts with the K-State rhizome measurements.
caveat: Italian climate; a mixture study, not a test of spread into bare spots.

title: Brown patch on tall fescue as influenced by nitrogen and fungicide applications
short: Fry 2025 (K-State): brown patch vs. nitrogen timing
authors: Fry J.D., Chhetri M. & Pease B.
takeaway: On July 21, 2023, plots fed 1.5 lb N/yr (September only) had 2–23% brown patch, while plots fed 4.5 lb (Sep, Nov, Apr, May) had 48–66%. The top-quality turf needed high nitrogen plus fungicide.
caveat: Irrigated plots with extra watering to encourage disease; nitrogen rate and spring timing were changed together.

title: Aboveground responses of cool-season lawn species to nitrogen rates and application timings
authors: Walker K.S., Bigelow C.A., Smith D.R., Van Scoyoc G.E. & Reicher Z.J.
takeaway: Tall fescue gave acceptable lawn quality at about 1.5–2.5 lb N/1,000 sq ft per year, less than many lawn programs apply.
caveat: Indiana (Purdue).

title: Fall fertilization timing effects on nitrate leaching and turfgrass color and growth
authors: Mangiafico S.S. & Guillard K.
takeaway: The later the fall application, the more nitrate leached, yet feedings anywhere from mid-October to mid-December gave the same color and density. Finish the last feeding by about mid-November.
caveat: Connecticut, on a bluegrass/fine fescue lawn.

title: Review of cool-season turfgrass water use and requirements: I. Evapotranspiration and responses to deficit irrigation
short: Braun 2022, part I: cool-season turf water use
authors: Braun R.C., Bremer D.J., Ebdon J.S., Fry J.D. & Patton A.J.
takeaway: Across studies, cool-season lawns needed only about 59–74% of full evapotranspiration to stay acceptable. That's why this site estimates lawn water use conservatively, at 0.8 × reference ET.
caveat: A review; the values vary by species, cultivar and site.

title: Review of cool-season turfgrass water use and requirements: II. Responses to drought stress
short: Braun 2022, part II: turf responses to drought
authors: Braun R.C., Bremer D.J., Ebdon J.S., Fry J.D. & Patton A.J.
takeaway: A review of how tall fescue, bluegrass and other cool-season grasses survive and recover from drought: tall fescue avoids drought with deep roots, while bluegrass tolerates dormancy and recovers from rhizomes.
caveat: A review, useful for background rather than a single decision.

title: Assessing the fertilizer and pesticide input needs of cool-season turfgrass species
short: Braun 2023: fertilizer & pesticide needs by species
authors: Braun R.C., Watkins E., Hollman A.B. & Patton A.J.
takeaway: In non-irrigated plots in Indiana and Minnesota, newer fine fescues needed 41–56% fewer inputs than tall fescue, bluegrass or ryegrass. They're worth considering for shady, low-traffic corners.
caveat: Northern sites; fine fescues struggle in hot, sunny KC summers.

title: Endophyte effects on drought tolerance of turf-type tall fescue
short: Boyle 2024: endophytes & tall fescue drought tolerance
authors: Boyle P.E., Richardson M.D., Karcher D.E., Hignight K.W., Hignight D. & Secks M.E.
takeaway: Endophyte infection had no consistent effect on tall fescue's drought response. "Endophyte-enhanced" on a seed tag is not a drought guarantee.
caveat: Endophytes can still help with some insects; this study was about drought only.

title: To mow or to mow less: Lawn mowing frequency affects bee abundance and diversity in suburban yards
authors: Lerman S.B., Contosta A.R., Milam J. & Bang C.
takeaway: In 16 Massachusetts yards, lawns mowed every 3 weeks had up to 2.5× more flowers, and lawns mowed every 2 weeks had the most bees. Mowing a little less often, rather than not at all, is what helped.
caveat: These were weedy lawns full of clover and dandelions, not a dense fescue stand.

title: No Mow May lawns have higher pollinator richness and abundances: An engaged community provides floral resources for pollinators
short: Del Toro 2020: No Mow May & pollinators
authors: Del Toro I. & Ribbons R.R.
takeaway: Retracted on Nov 18, 2022, over "several potential inconsistencies in data handling and reporting." This is the study that launched "No Mow May," and it can't be cited as evidence.
caveat: The retraction doesn't prove that mowing less is bad; see Lerman 2018 and Hemmings 2022.

title: No-mow amenity grassland case study: Phenology of floral abundance and nectar resource
authors: Hemmings K., Elton R. & Grange I.
takeaway: Unmown grassland produced more nectar, but the difference only showed up in mid-to-late May and peaked (8×) in June.
caveat: One UK grassland, not a tall fescue lawn. For a KC lawn, mowing tall and leaving flowers in beds or a clover patch does more for pollinators than skipping May.

title: Mulched maple and oak leaves associated with a reduction in common dandelion populations in established Kentucky bluegrass
authors: Kowalewski A.R., Buhler D.D., Lang N.S., Nair M.G. & Rogers J.N.
takeaway: Mowing fall leaves into the lawn (about 0.3 lb per sq ft) cut dandelions by up to 80% after one year and improved spring green-up. Maple and oak worked equally well.
caveat: Michigan State, on a bluegrass lawn with dandelion seed added on purpose.

title: Degree-days for predicting smooth crabgrass emergence in cool-season turfgrasses
authors: Fidanza M.A., Dernoeden P.H. & Zhang M.
takeaway: Soil temperature at 1 in was the best predictor. The first crabgrass seedlings appeared after a week averaging 57–63.5°F, and big flushes came when soil averaged above 73°F.
caveat: Maryland, 1992–94.

title: Phenological indicators for emergence of large and smooth crabgrass
short: Cardina 2011: bloom cues for crabgrass emergence
authors: Cardina J., Herms C.P. & Herms D.A.
takeaway: Published degree-day models missed actual crabgrass emergence by up to 60+ days, but the order in which landscape plants bloomed was a consistent guide. That's why "apply at redbud bloom" works.
caveat: Ohio.

title: Weed control and turf safety of single and sequential applications of herbicides over spring seedings
authors: Sousek M.D., Gaussoin R.E., Patton A.J., Weisenberger D.V. & Reicher Z.J.
takeaway: Mesotrione gave consistent weed control without hurting spring-seeded tall fescue or bluegrass. The authors still "strongly" recommend late-summer to early-fall seeding.
caveat: Nebraska and Indiana.

title: Weed control options in spring-seeded tall fescue
short: Willis 2006: weeds in spring-seeded tall fescue
authors: Willis J.B., Beam J.B., Barker W.L. & Askew S.D.
takeaway: Sequential mesotrione applications controlled smooth crabgrass without injuring spring-seeded tall fescue.
caveat: Virginia.

title: 2018 National Tall Fescue Test, final report 2019–23 (NTEP No. 24-9)
takeaway: Transition-zone mean quality (9 sites, LSD 0.3): Daybreak 6.4; Titanium G-LS, Capitan, Providence, Titan GLX and Spyder 2LS 6.3; Kentucky-31 4.4. At the non-irrigated Manhattan, KS site: Titan GLX and Xanadu 5.5, Hellcat GLR 5.4, Triad 5.3. At Columbia, MO: Spyder 2LS and Xanadu 6.4, Titanium G-LS 6.3.

title: 2024 National Tall Fescue Test, progress report (NTEP No. 26-1)
takeaway: 108 entries, including Kansas sites. The first year of data is out; results firm up over the next few years.

title: NTEP Turfgrass Trial Explorer
takeaway: Map-based tool for comparing NTEP cultivar results by trial site, including the 2018 tall fescue test (2019–23).

title: Turfgrass Water Conservation Alliance: qualified tall fescues
takeaway: Cultivars qualify by holding green cover under drought stress at every test site for at least 2 years; seed carrying the TWCA seal must be at least 70% qualified seed. The list includes Aquavita, Rebel V, Rebel Xpedition, Thunderstruck, GLX Aced, Lifeguard, RainDance and others.

title: U.S. Climate Normals 1991–2020: Kansas City International Airport (USW00003947)
org: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
takeaway: 39.30 in of rain a year (wettest May–June), 36.3 days ≥90°F. Median last 32°F freeze April 13 (1-in-10 after April 29); median first 32°F freeze October 24 (1-in-10 before October 9).

title: Frost dates for Kansas City, Missouri
takeaway: Probability view of frost dates. It uses the warmer Downtown Airport station, whose median first fall frost (Nov 2) is about 9 days later than KCI's (Oct 24).

title: Crop Evapotranspiration: Guidelines for Computing Crop Water Requirements (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56)
org: Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN
authors: Allen R.G., Pereira L.S., Raes D. & Smith M.
takeaway: The reference evapotranspiration (ET₀) method that the weather model uses; lawn water use = a crop coefficient × ET₀.

title: Open-Meteo free weather API
takeaway: Free, key-free forecast and recent-weather data (temperature, rain, soil temperature, evapotranspiration) behind the live alerts.

title: Missouri Revised Statutes §640.648: right to rainwater collection systems
takeaway: "All Missouri landowners retain the right to have, use, and own systems for rainwater collection anytime and anywhere on their own property, including land within city limits."

title: The product label
takeaway: The label is the law. Rates, reseeding intervals, re-entry times, pollinator warnings and "don't use on" lists are legally binding and override any calendar, including this one.

title: Community Collaborative Rain, Hail & Snow Network
takeaway: Volunteers report daily rain from a standard 4-inch gauge; you can also see neighbors' readings to check your own.

title: Missouri One Call System (811)
takeaway: Free utility locates before you dig: tree planting, fence posts, deep edging. Missouri law requires notice before excavating.

title: Master Gardeners of Greater Kansas City
takeaway: Local volunteer experts: garden hotline, demonstration gardens, classes and soil-test drop-off help.

title: Kansas City Community Gardens
takeaway: Low-cost seeds and transplants, classes and community garden plots around Kansas City.
